applicability: A routing table, row count, or slot cursor needs one value rather than a tile.
Several SPMD blocks or `pl.parallel` instances write different elements of one output.
A scatter must be coherent across cores.
directions: Partition `pld`/tensor writes so each instance writes a contiguous run aligned to and sized in whole 64-byte lines.
Use `pl.spmd(1)` when only one instance should write a control tensor.
Use `pl.store(partial, [0, 0], out, atomic=pl.AtomicType.Add)` into a zeroed output for split-K-style cross-core accumulation.
Use `pl.array.create(N, pl.INT32)` for a per-instance cursor and `pl.array.create(N, pl.TASK_ID)` for a TaskId fan-in.
Cast a scalar read used as an offset or loop bound to `pl.INDEX`.
effects: Scalar access is convenient for control values but incurs cache-line granularity and per-access cost.
Whole-line partitioning may waste bytes at the end of a run but preserves correctness.
Atomics avoid line ownership but make floating-point accumulation order non-deterministic and require a zeroed destination.
invariants: Atomic-add destinations must be zero-initialized before the kernel.
Supported atomic-add tile dtypes are fp32, bf16, fp16, int32, int16, and int8; bf16 atomic-add is documented for 910B/A2/A3 but not A5.
A scalar loop over a tile-sized region is much slower than the corresponding vector op.
`pl.write` returns an IR expression; the DSL parser surfaces it as an `EvalStmt`.
`pl.array.create(extent, dtype)` supports integer, BOOL, or TASK_ID elements, requires a compile-time constant extent, is private to the creating block, and does not cross function boundaries.
principle: `pl.load`/`pl.store` move a tile by DMA. `pl.read`/`pl.write` move one element through the issuing core's data cache. A scalar write reaches DDR as a whole 64-byte cache line when the kernel ends, and different cores' caches are not kept coherent within a task. Two instances that write different elements in the same 64-byte line can each write back their own copy of all 64 bytes, so the last write-back wins and the other store disappears. The rule is that each instance must own whole 64-byte lines: 16 elements for INT32/FP32, 32 for FP16/BF16, 8 for INT64, and 64 for INT8. Within one instance there is no hazard because it runs sequentially on one core. The hazard applies to `pl.spmd(n)` with `n > 1` and to `for ... in pl.parallel(n)` instances the runtime may overlap. `ScalarWriteLineShared` warns when the compiler cannot prove whole-line ownership; it names the measured stride when it can analyze the index, and reports that a runtime index is unanalyzable otherwise. The warning is a question for a runtime index, not a verdict; if the layout invariant is real and documented, it can be disabled with `disabled_diagnostics`. Two different tasks writing one tensor are not reported, because their temporal overlap is unknown. A write guarded by `if blk == 0` is still reported conservatively because the check does not read predicates. Use `pl.spmd(1)` for a handful of control values, a per-instance scratch row for partial results, or `pl.store(..., atomic=pl.AtomicType.Add)` into a zero-initialized destination for a true cross-core scatter. Atomic-add order is not fixed, so floating-point results are non-deterministic. `pl.array.create(extent, dtype)` creates a small core-local array for cursors or TaskId fan-in; its extent must be compile-time constant, and updates are functional. A scalar read of a tensor is also legal in orchestration, where a device-computed count can become a host-side loop bound after casting to `pl.INDEX`.
questions: The exact cache coherence behavior for a particular mixed AIC/AIV handoff depends on the generated cache-maintenance sequence.
risks: A grid-stride loop where 16 blocks each write one element of the same INT32 line; most stores vanish and the surviving set varies between runs.
Believing `if blk == 0` suppresses `ScalarWriteLineShared`; the check is not predicate-aware.
Using a scalar read as a loop bound without an `INT64`/`pl.INDEX` cast.
Assuming scalar writes from different tasks are coherent without a cache publication/invalidation sequence.
Treating `pl.array` as shared across blocks or as mutable in place; it is block-local and updates rebind functionally.
summary: `pl.read`/`pl.write` reach one element through the issuing core's data cache, and cache write-back happens in whole 64-byte lines. Concurrent task instances must own whole lines; disjoint element indices are not enough.
title: Scalar Access and the 64-Byte Write Granularity
